# Research R404 — layer-major FP32 RAM bridge copy contract and DMA evidence

Date: 2026-10-13 (Asia/Tokyo)

## Scope and provenance

Read-only review requested for the FP32 residual bridge in the current frozen layer-major candidate. Machine context supplied for this inquiry: Intel Arc B570 10 GiB, Ryzen 5 5600X, 128 GiB RAM, observed upstream link about 6 GB/s. The canonical source tree is `/home/yayoi/ghq/github.com/yqYo1/Strata/.worktree/feat-phase-gated-quality-capture-20261013` at clean commit `b4f7b5ec1d7583de52f0e0dbcf181d461591cf17`. The live candidate is `/home/yayoi/ghq/github.com/yqYo1/Strata/.worktree/feat-restore-layer-major-prefill-20261013`, HEAD `8b48d17c99b70d32781f9f5b056602a598a37b1c`; it was already dirty at inspection, with tracked edits in layer/session/prefill/generate and phase cache test files plus untracked layer-major header/docs. Those candidate changes were explicitly incomplete/live. No file in either source worktree was changed by this review; no lint, build, test, AST, model, process, GPU, or profiler work was performed.

The candidate source files were SHA-256 hashed before and after this review; matching hashes are recorded below. `git status --short` was checked before and after and remained at the pre-existing dirty state. Only this report was written. The current feature has not executed an L-model request. An earlier first-row diagnostic's 248,320 FP32 logits are not evidence for layer-major bridge correctness or quality.

## Finding: ordinary host pointers are valid copy endpoints

In candidate `src/prefill/prefill.cpp`, `run_layer_major` allocates the host-tail residual plane with `std::vector<float> rows`, sets `m.residual_host = rows.data()`, and keeps that vector alive for the full invocation. Its per-layer chunk callback sends device residual `residual` to either the GPU-prefix plane or the pageable `rows` tail with synchronous `gpu::copy(output, residual, bytes)`. For layers after the first, `run_impl` submits pageable host-tail-to-device `gpu::copy_async(m.R, input, bytes, m.cs)` before the layer kernels. These are copies through the compute queue; the helper implementation is queue `memcpy`, with `copy` waiting for the returned event and `copy_async` returning after submission.

Khronos SYCL 2020 revision 12, §4.9.4.3, explicitly permits each `handler::memcpy` endpoint to be a host pointer or an accessible same-context USM pointer. Therefore `std::vector` storage is a legal endpoint for these explicit copy commands. It does not need to be pinned or USM for copy correctness. That rule does not make the pointer legal for direct device-kernel dereference: kernel access is a USM/accessibility question. A pageable source may incur implementation-managed staging or other slower transfer behavior, but the spec does not require a particular registration, pinning, import, or performance path.

For asynchronous H2D, the host row bytes must remain allocated and unmodified until the command has finished reading them. The candidate's `rows` owner lasts past the request and the callback does not rewrite the residual plane; queue order places the submitted H2D before dependent compute on `m.cs`. The synchronous D2H `gpu::copy` waits before returning, so its destination rows are complete before later host use. Candidate teardown drains compute/copy queues before restoring owners. These are source-level ordering observations, not proof of runtime behavior under an executed request. Level Zero's `zeCommandListAppendMemoryCopy` contract similarly allows host, device, or shared memory and specifies that the implementation accesses endpoints only on execution; the application must keep the memory valid and avoid modifying it while the command can read/write it.

Host-USM would be needed for a design that directly exposes host storage to device kernels or wants a known USM allocation classification. It is not required just to call queue memcpy on ordinary host pointers. Pinned/registered memory and host-USM must also remain distinct: registration can enable transfer use without making a pointer an ordinary kernel-accessible USM allocation.

Primary API references:

- Khronos, [SYCL 2020 Specification revision 12, §4.9.4.3](https://registry.khronos.org/SYCL/specs/sycl-2020/pdf/sycl-2020.pdf), pp. 320–321 (host pointer or accessible same-context USM for memcpy).
- Intel, [Level Zero command-list memory copy](https://oneapi-src.github.io/level-zero-spec/level-zero/latest/core/api/apis/command_list.html#zecommandlistappendmemorycopy) (host/device/shared endpoint and execution-time access/lifetime contract).
- Intel, [Level Zero Core Programming Guide: access capabilities](https://oneapi-src.github.io/level-zero-spec/level-zero/latest/core/PROG.html#access-capabilities) (host allocation accessibility/concurrency is a separate allocation capability; no such capability is needed to copy an ordinary pointer).

## What the ~6 GB/s receipt measures

The committed Git receipt is from `bench/results/2026-10-10-hardware-architecture-decisions/component-capacity-matrix-v2.json`, SHA-256 `fbcaf9a0c9e268ae43c388b321d9c3c22599e188fbbb1fca88a9356fc07186b3`. It points to `bench/results/2026-10-10-parallel-round54/hardware/validated-three-process-summary.json`, SHA-256 `21a86b9324f0b28a08fc4790661fd9a44bac8f63d943e818b7586082e5b49a29`, committed snapshot `0e55471bf4618e02d4ac3acfd91c72380a8d974b`. The measurement source is `/home/yayoi/.local/state/strata-sycl/post-reboot-tuning-20261007/hardware_ceiling_gpu_v1.cpp`, SHA-256 `6f27814b78d076c1c1dd9d75e3d7285c89190ca54e7c4bb5cda11388fa200e1c`.

That probe uses a B570 Level Zero in-order SYCL queue, profiling disabled, 256 MiB buffers, seven timed samples per case in each of three fresh GPU processes. For each timed sample it submits four 256 MiB queue memcpy calls (1 GiB logical one-way payload), brackets submission with a host `steady_clock`, and waits for the queue before stopping the timer. The reported table is the median of the three process medians and the range of those process medians. `malloc_host` buffers define the Host-USM cases; `std::malloc` buffers define pageable cases. Copies are fully content-validated. Thus 6.446834 GB/s is attained effective one-way payload throughput for 256 MiB H2D from a `sycl::malloc_host` allocation with host-inclusive submit-and-completion timing, not a PCIe protocol-counter rate, not a raw DMA-engine-only interval, and not the candidate's layer/chunk copy rate.

The same receipt reports Host-USM D2H 5.642946 GB/s, pageable H2D 4.605214 GB/s, and pageable D2H 5.273931 GB/s, also for 256 MiB one-way payload. The benchmark README states GPU durations include host submission and completion wait, profiling is disabled, and simultaneous CPU staging/DMA/compute was not measured. The companion physical-path receipt (`physical-bandwidth-reference.json`, SHA-256 `5bd8ccdfe50bdfe6f3afaf68d4861ac831ae54dc49eb7c9b8fd4f716d4d834fc`) records a Gen4x4 external path; the ideal 128/130-encoded arithmetic is 7.876923 GB/s per direction before packet overhead. That is a topology/encoding upper envelope, not the observed 6.446834 rate and not a guarantee for arbitrary host pointers.

This evidence makes the pageable results the more relevant existing transfer control for the current `std::vector` bridge, but still not a direct prediction: the test uses 256 MiB large copies, whereas prompt copies are chunk-sized (and may be much smaller), and the layer-major path's exact queue dependencies and whole-request interference have not been measured. Ordinary pageable memory can be copied correctly while attaining a lower rate than host-USM. No receipt demonstrates that the candidate's H2D/D2H follows either microbenchmark path at its measured rate.

## Logical bridge size and capacity limits

The layer-major layout uses `D = 10,240` FP32 elements per residual row, i.e. 40,960 bytes per position. `plan.host_bytes = (tokens - gpu_tokens) * D * 4`. At 262,144 positions with zero GPU prefix this is 10,737,418,240 bytes (10 GiB) in the pageable host vector. A GPU prefix reduces the host tail by exactly `gpu_tokens * 40,960` bytes, subject to the plan's chunk-rounded prefix. This host capacity is separate from the transfer payload: under the all-host-tail 262,144-position scenario, each of 47 intermediate layer boundaries logically moves 10 GiB D2H and 10 GiB H2D, or 504,658,657,280 bytes per direction across the request. At 32,768 positions, the analogous all-host-tail amounts are 1.25 GiB per boundary and 63,082,332,160 bytes per direction for 47 boundaries. These are static scenario counts, not a claim that a request was run or that PCIe physically carried those bytes.

Candidate admission checks `host_bytes + MAXBLOB + layers*experts*sizeof(int32_t) + reserve` against available host memory, and checks vector `max_size`, overflow, and allocation exceptions. The GPU-prefix extent plus one-layer cache plus reserve is checked against fresh reported free VRAM; each layer blob must fit the chosen max slot. That is useful capacity gating, but available system RAM is not a pinned-memory budget, and the reviewed bridge does not query USM host max allocation or guarantee a single 10 GiB host-USM allocation would succeed. Nor does a nominal 10 GiB host plane establish a 10 GiB pinned allowance. Any pinned design needs allocation-size and failure guards, a bounded fallback, and an explicit host-memory budget; do not treat pinning the entire context plane as automatically safe.

R267's existing conditional worksheet reports 47-boundary all-host-tail 32K payload at the measured pageable rates as 13.698 s H2D + 11.961 s D2H = 25.659 s, with no overlap. Those are payload/rate divisions, not elapsed candidate time. At full 262,144 positions the host vector alone is 10 GiB; physical device capacity is 10,666,115,072 bytes (9.936 GiB), so that full residual plane cannot be placed entirely on this B570 even before other allocations. A host-backed design avoids that device-capacity contradiction but does not remove H2D/D2H byte traffic. No model-level fit, correctness, speed, or physical-transfer claim follows from these arithmetic bounds.

## Candidate ranking for the pageable bridge

1. **Keep the full residual tail pageable as the bounded-capacity baseline; first attribute actual chunk copies.** The current `std::vector<float>` design allows the maximum 10 GiB plane without requiring a monolithic pinned allocation. Preserve its available-RAM admission and exception/failure handling. Before any speed conclusion, a matched model request must count completed residual H2D/D2H bytes by chunk and record copy completion service separately from queue wait and wall time. Do not multiply logical bytes by the ~6 GB/s Host-USM sample and label it measured service.
2. **If transfer evidence justifies it, compare a bounded pinned bounce buffer, not a 10 GiB pinned bridge.** Allocate one or a small number of `malloc_host` buffers sized to the maximum active chunk (`T * D * sizeof(float)`, after overflow/max-size/device allocation guards). For H2D, copy the pageable row slice into the bounce buffer, enqueue H2D, and do not overwrite/reuse that slot until its completion event. For D2H, copy into the pinned slot, wait for the D2H event, then copy into pageable rows before returning the slot. Keep slot count and bytes explicit and the single-buffer synchronous fallback valid. This bounds pinned residency independently from full context, but adds a CPU copy in each direction and one event/wait discipline; the existing synthetic RAM copy rate is not evidence that this bridge will win. Compare actual 1/2/3 chunk-slot cases only after a timer-off matched model baseline and source/status preservation.
3. **Do not choose a full-plane Host-USM allocation solely from its 6.447 GB/s result.** That allocation changes memory kind and pinning pressure for a 10 GiB full-context tail, may fail device/context allocation limits, and has not been shown to be eligible within current host budget. If investigated, split it into bounded allocations or preflight actual maximum-allocation and host-budget constraints with a clean fallback. Host-USM may remove internal pageable staging, but does not make a host-resident residual directly kernel-accessible in any arbitrary allocation, guarantee concurrent host/device access, or prove that chunk copies become faster.

The first follow-up should keep all correctness/status accounting intact, measure full completed copy chains for the actual layer/chunk geometry, and report pageable/direct host-USM/bounded-bounce separately. Retain each rate's operation and allocation semantics. A whole-request comparison is needed before promoting an option because measured component rates alone do not establish critical-path exposure or overlap.
